analysis.one_liner: Requires hospitals and doctors to give patients a list of services at discharge and at least 30 business days to pay bills.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in May 2019 and referred to the Senate health committee, which never took it up; it died when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021 with no hearing, no vote, and one cosponsor.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require hospitals and health care practitioners to give patients a list of the services rendered before they leave, to send all bills within 30 business days, and to leave patients at least 30 business days to pay after receiving a bill. Providers who bill outside the window would have to report the bill to the Department of Health and Human Services and refund the patient in full with interest, and a provider sending more than 10 late bills could face civil fines of up to $10,000 per day. It would not cap what providers charge — it only sets rules for how and when patients are billed.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients, especially those facing unexpected or slow-arriving medical bills. Anyone who has received a bill months after a visit, been pressed for quick payment, or been billed for services they can't identify would get an itemized service list at discharge, a firm deadline by which bills must arrive, a guaranteed window to pay, and a full refund with interest if a provider bills late. Insurers and employers who process medical bills would also get more predictable timing.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Patients with unexpected or late medical bills

how_it_helps.text: Facilities and practitioners must give patients a list of services rendered at the time of discharge, so patients can check what they are being charged for [S2][S3].

All bills must be sent within 30 business days, and no patient can be required to pay sooner than 30 business days after receiving a bill, ending surprise billing timing and payment pressure [S2][S3].
A provider who bills outside the window must report the bill to the Department of Health and Human Services and refund the full amount paid, with interest [S2][S3].
A provider that sends more than 10 late bills can face civil monetary penalties of up to $10,000 per day, enforced through the existing Medicare penalty process [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Hospitals, clinics, and individual practitioners, who would carry the cost of producing itemized service lists at discharge and restructuring their billing timelines, plus refunds with interest and potential fines for late billing. Small practices could face proportionally heavier compliance burdens than large systems, and providers' revenue timing would slow since bills cannot go out and cannot be collected within 30 business days of service.

drawbacks.text: The bill regulates when and how patients are billed, not what providers charge — an itemized list of an overpriced service is still an overpriced bill, and the bill would do nothing about the underlying prices [S2].

The compliance burden falls on all facilities and practitioners, and small practices would have to build itemized-discharge and 30-day billing systems with the same deadlines as large hospital chains; a provider sending more than 10 late bills could face fines of up to $10,000 per day [S3].

Pushing every bill out to at least a 60-business-day span (30 to bill, 30 to pay) would slow cash flow to providers, a cost that could be passed on in prices or absorbed in smaller practices' margins [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to patients is real but narrow: this is a billing-timing and disclosure bill, not a price or surprise-out-of-network-billing bill, so it would not lower anyone's bill. The costs — compliance for providers and slower payment timing — are modest and mostly borne by the entities being regulated. On balance a reasonable consumer protection, though far from the bigger medical-billing problems (surprise out-of-network bills and high prices) that larger, competing bills in the same Congress addressed.

outcome.mechanism: It was read twice and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never acted on it before Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Enzi introduced the bill on May 23, 2019, joined by one Democratic cosponsor, Senator Casey [S1][S4].
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee [S1][S5].
No further action appears in the record — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor action — and the bill died when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Hospitals and medical providers are better off because the bill never moved: their billing timelines, service-list practices, and revenue timing stay exactly as they were, with no refunds-with-interest obligation or daily fines for late bills. Patients facing slow or confusing medical bills gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Hospitals and providers whose billing goes unchanged

for.name: Sen. Michael Enzi
for.role: Sponsor; former chairman of the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the HELP Committee, where he had long served

against.name: Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.role: Committee of referral; chaired by Sen. Lamar Alexander (R-TN) in the 116th Congress
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or vote on the bill, leaving it to die at the end of the Congress

sides.party_line_note: A Republican senator sponsored the bill with a single Democratic cosponsor, but the partisan split is irrelevant here — the bill never got far enough to divide either party, since the Senate committee of referral took no action in the 20 months after introduction.

industries.note: The bill would force itemized service lists at discharge, 30-business-day billing deadlines, refunds with interest for late bills, and fines up to $10,000 per day for repeat late billers. Hospitals profit from billing practices that arrive late and are hard for patients to parse, so the bill's rules run against their current revenue practices.

The same billing deadlines, refund, and penalty rules apply to individual practitioners, and small practices would bear the compliance burden alongside large systems. Faster service-item disclosures would help their patients understand charges but slow the practices' own collections.
The bill guarantees patients at least 30 business days after receiving a bill before any payment can be demanded, cutting into aggressive early-collections and payment-pressure tactics.
